entities.summary:
Maykop, the capital city of the Republic of Adygea, Russia, is situated on the right bank of the Belaya River, a tributary of the Kuban. While its modern urban history dates to the mid-19th century as a Russian military outpost founded in 1857, its greatest historical significance stems from the eponymous Maykop culture, a major archaeological phenomenon of the Early Bronze Age (c. 3700–3000 BCE) in the North Caucasus. This ancient culture, named after the discovery of a spectacular royal kurgan (burial mound) in the city in 1897, represents a pivotal moment in the development of metallurgy and social complexity across Eurasia.

The Maykop culture is renowned for its advanced bronze technology, sophisticated gold and silver craftsmanship, and elaborate burial practices, particularly the kurgan burials of its elite. The Maykop kurgan itself, excavated by Nikolai Veselovsky, yielded an astonishing array of artifacts, including gold and silver vessels, bronze tools, and intricate jewelry, demonstrating a high degree of social stratification and specialized artisanry. These finds provided crucial insights into early metallurgical techniques, including alloying and casting, which were among the most sophisticated of their time in the broader Pontic-Caspian steppe and Caucasus regions. The culture's economic base likely included cattle breeding and agriculture, supported by its fertile riverine location.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Maykop is historically significant primarily as the namesake and type-site for the Maykop culture (c. 3700–3000 BCE), which pioneered advanced metallurgy and social stratification in the North Caucasus and influenced subsequent Bronze Age societies across Eurasia.
